props.title: Where Is the Friend's Home?

sections.content: Abbas Kiarostami's **Where Is the Friend's Home?** (1987) revolutionized Iranian cinema with its deceptively simple story of a young boy's determined quest to return his classmate's notebook. The film established Kiarostami's signature style of blending documentary-like realism with poetic storytelling, influencing later works like Close-Up (1990) and **Through the Olive Trees** (1994). Its patient observation of childhood determination echoes in later masterpieces like Majid Majidi's **Children of Heaven** (1997), while its moral complexity and focus on everyday Iranian life created a template for the Iranian New Wave.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond Iranian borders, establishing a model for humanist cinema that depicts children's perspectives without sentimentality. Its DNA can be found in Jafar Panahi's **The White Balloon** (1995), Asghar Farhadi's **A Separation** (2011), and even non-Iranian works like Hirokazu Kore-eda's **Nobody Knows** (2004). Kiarostami's technique of using non-professional actors and real locations, while following a child's unwavering moral compass, created a new language for depicting youth on screen.

The film's meticulous attention to geographical and social detail transforms a simple journey into a profound exploration of rural Iranian society. This approach influenced later neo-realist works like Samira Makhmalbaf's **The Apple** (1998) and Bahman Ghobadi's **A Time for Drunken Horses** (2000). Kiarostami's use of long takes and repetitive journeys would become hallmarks of contemplative cinema, seen in works like The Wind Will Carry Us (1999) and **Certified Copy** (2010). SUBHEAD: Impact on Global Cinema

movies.title: Close-Up
movies.slug: Kiarostami's meta-documentary about a man who impersonated filmmaker Mohsen Makhmalbaf

sections.content: The film's success at international festivals helped establish Iranian cinema's global reputation, paving the way for directors like Mohsen Makhmalbaf with **Gabbeh** (1996) and later Asghar Farhadi with **About Elly** (2009). Its influence on depicting childhood extends to contemporary works like Nadine Labaki's **Capernaum** (2018) and Zar Amir Ebrahimi's **Holy Spider** (2022), showing how Kiarostami's humanist approach continues to resonate.
